bc_cougar_canyon.blurb: Cougar Canyon is a gneiss canyon on the east side of Kalamalka Lake, in the Vernon end of the Okanagan. Sport routes make up most of the climbing, with a healthy share of trad and a little bouldering and top-roping. Grades centre on 5.9 to 5.11, with plenty of 5.10s, a few easier leads and only a handful of 5.12s. The rock is grainy and textured, comparable in character to Skaha although the canyon is smaller. Creekside Wall and Toad Hall are the gentle end of the canyon, good for newer leaders, while Beta Wall and Gamma Wall are where the steeper, harder lines are found. Walls are spread along the canyon rather than packed into one cliff.

ca_druid_stones.blurb: Druid Stones is a bouldering-only zone in the foothills southwest of Bishop, perched roughly 2,000 feet above the Owens Valley with views of the Sierra crest. The rock is coarse monzonite, the same as at the Buttermilks, so it is sharp on skin. Problems run from easy warm-ups through to a few double-digit testpieces, with the bulk between V0 and V4 and a fair number of V5 to V8. Many lines are highball, so extra pads are worth carrying up the steep, sandy 25 to 45 minute hike. It sees far fewer people than the main Bishop venues. Early spring, autumn and cool summer mornings suit it best. The Otherworld, Druid Stone Area and Long Ship Area hold the most problems.

co_carter_lake.blurb: Carter Lake is a bouldering destination along roughly a mile of the east bank of a foothills reservoir in Larimer County, at about 5,960 feet and around 45 minutes from Boulder. Every climb here is a boulder problem. Grades lean easy and moderate, with a large block of V0 to V3, a solid group at V4 and V5, and a handful of V8 and V10 for the strong. Most problems sit a little up from the water. Landings are uneven enough to be hard on ankles, though not dangerous. The area is split into dozens of small boulders and walls, with Extension Boulder, Kahuna Boulder, Big Block and Chain Rock among the larger ones.

co_north_cheyenne_canyon_2.blurb: North Cheyenne Canyon is a city park in southwest Colorado Springs, with climbing scattered along the canyon road, not always right beside it. The rock is Pikes Peak granite, and quality improves the farther up the canyon you go. Sport routes and boulder problems are about equally common, with a good amount of trad and a few top-ropes. Roped grades sit mostly between 5.7 and 5.11, with a few 5.12s and 5.13s, and the boulders run from easy to a couple of very hard problems. In winter the canyon also holds some ice and mixed climbing. Notable spots are The Pinnacle, Silver Cascade Slab, The Amphitheater and Buzzard Boulders.

_expect.name: North Fork of the St. Vrain River

co_north_fork_of_the_st_vrain_river.blurb: The North Fork is one of the three drainages of the St. Vrain canyons west of Lyons, the one reached from the US 36 side. The St. Vrain canyons as a whole are granitic and mostly good quality, though some rock is coarse or loose. Here the climbing is split fairly evenly between boulders, trad and sport. Most roped routes fall between 5.9 and 5.13, with 5.10 the most common, and the boulders run from V0 to V9 with a few harder. The Longmont Reservoir area, also called Buttonrock, holds steep sport and crack climbing on formations that face different ways, so it can be climbed through much of the year when it is dry. Big Elk Meadows boulders, Button Rock and Raven's Roost add variety.

ma_sector_two.blurb: Sector Two is the larger of the two main sectors of the Promised Land, a boulder-filled corner of Lynn Woods on the North Shore. Almost all of the climbing is bouldering, with only a few trad lines. The Promised Land is known for granite blocks about 10 to 20 feet tall packed into short, close-together clusters, and the problems here are weighted toward V3 to V6, with some easier lines and a few V7 and V8. The Tower Boulders sit behind a tower on a hill, get a little sun but are mostly shaded by pines. Hillside Area, Forgotten Boulders and Upper Quarry Boulders are among the larger groups.
